title: Inquiry says ‘yes’ to ESL reform but ‘not sure’ on model
full_text:
Inquiry says ‘yes’ to ESL reform but ‘not sure’ on model
An inquiry has recommended the next NSW parliament move ahead with decoupling the emergency services levy from insurance, but a replacement model remains unclear.
In May, a parliamentary select committee called for submissions on a Treasury paper presenting property-based alternatives involving a tiered approach.
“The committee found that there was strong stakeholder support for reforming the current ESL,” the committee’s final report says.
“However, there was no clear consensus of support for any of the five possible levy options outlined in the options paper.”
The report backs reform to improve insurance affordability and rectify a situation where people without cover make no direct financial contribution to emergency services funding, even as they benefit.
The next parliament should adopt a replacement levy that is equitable, efficient, simple and sustainable, and the inquiry report should be considered in developing the new arrangement, the committee recommends.
Pensioners and vulnerable community members should be protected, with Revenue NSW responsible for collecting and administering any replacement levy, the report says.
The next state election is on March 13.
The Insurance Council of Australia says the committee’s unanimous recommendation to replace the ESL means reform has bipartisan support.
“Whoever forms government after March, the people of NSW should be confident that both sides of politics now agree this tax is unfair and must go, and the next parliament needs to make delivering a fairer way to fund emergency services an early priority,” CEO Andrew Hall said.
“Beyond the bipartisan recommendations, One Nation has also committed to removing taxes from insurance, so there is growing support to get this done.”
The committee was chaired by independent MP Jacqui Scruby and included representatives from Labor, the Liberals, Nationals and Greens.
ICA says the industry looks forward to all parties committing to legislating the reform early in the next term, and it is ready to work with the incoming government on a fair and orderly transition.
The Property Council of Australia says moving the levy off insurance does not make the cost disappear, and the question it has weighed is where that bill lands next.
“The committee has recognised the fundamental principle we have been arguing for: the cost needs to be spread equitably across the community and particularly that industrial and commercial owners should not be adversely impacted by a replacement levy,” NSW executive director Katie Stevenson said.
